title: Most people assume Judas looked evil from the beginning.
paragraphs: Most people assume Judas looked evil from the beginning.
Like betrayal always arrives wearing darkness.
But Scripture paints something far more terrifying.
Judas looked trustworthy.

Calm.
Capable.
Disciplined.
Reliable enough that the other disciples trusted him with the ministry finances.
And that should shake every religious person reading this.
Because it means proximity to Jesus is not the same as surrender to Jesus.
You can carry the money bag and still carry secret sin.
You can preach Christ and still love silver.
You can walk beside miracles while your heart slowly rots in silence.
God saw it.
And Judas knew.
The first major revelation comes from the Gospel of John.

“But Judas Iscariot, one of His disciples (he who was about to betray Him), said, ‘Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?’ He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.”
— John 12:4–6 (ESV)
The Greek text is devastatingly precise.
The phrase:
“having charge of the moneybag”
comes from:

τὸ γλωσσόκομον ἔχων
(to glōssokomon echōn)

The word γλωσσόκομον (glōssokomon) originally referred to a small box used to store the reeds of musical instruments, but by the first century it had evolved into a term for a money chest or treasury bag.
Judas was not casually holding spare coins.
He was functioning as the group treasurer.

Trusted.
Established.
Official.
And notice something else.
The disciples apparently never suspected him.
Even during the Last Supper, when Jesus announced betrayal, nobody immediately pointed at Judas.
Instead they asked:

“Is it I, Lord?”
— Matthew 26:22
That means Judas had successfully maintained an image of spiritual legitimacy.

That is one of the central warnings of Scripture:
external faithfulness can conceal internal corruption.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus knew from the beginning.
Not eventually.
From the start.
In John 6:64, Jesus says:
“But there are some of you who do not believe.”
Then John explains:
“For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray Him.”
The Greek phrase:

ἐξ ἀρχῆς
(ex archēs)
means “from the beginning,” “from the outset,” “from the origin.”
Christ was never deceived by Judas’ appearance.
Humans were.
God was not.
Then Jesus says something even more shocking:

“Did I not choose you, the Twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”
— John 6:70
The Greek word used here is:
διάβολος (diabolos)

Meaning:
“slanderer,”
“accuser,”
or one who acts in the character of the devil.
This does not mean Judas was literally Satan himself.
It means his heart had aligned itself with satanic rebellion while still walking among the disciples.
That should terrify anyone who thinks religious performance equals salvation.
So why did the disciples trust Judas with the money?
Because Judas probably excelled in areas people admire.

Competence.
Administration.
Organization.
Presentation.
Scripture never portrays him as chaotic or reckless outwardly.
In fact, he likely appeared more financially responsible than some of the others.
Remember who some disciples were:

Peter was impulsive.
John was deeply emotional.
Matthew had been a tax collector with a controversial past.
Several were fishermen with little indication of financial administration.
Judas may have seemed naturally suited for stewardship.
And this reveals something deeply important about human nature:
people often mistake gifting for godliness.
The church still does this today.

Someone speaks well.
Leads efficiently.
Handles systems effectively.
Knows Scripture intellectually.
So people assume spiritual maturity.
But talent can hide decay.
Jesus warned about this repeatedly.
In Matthew 7:22–23:
“Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name…?’”
And Jesus responds:
“I never knew you.”

Not:
“I knew you once.”
“I never knew you.”
The Greek phrase:

οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
(oudepote egnōn hymas)

means:
“Never at any time did I truly know you relationally.”
Religious activity is not proof of redemption.
Judas is the living warning.
Now we must ask the harder question.
Why would Jesus allow Judas to keep the money bag if He knew Judas was stealing?
Because Christ was exposing something bigger than theft.
He was revealing the true condition of the human heart.
Judas was not ruined by opportunity.
Opportunity revealed what already lived inside him.
That is a biblical pattern.

Money does not create greed.
Power does not create corruption.
Temptation exposes worship.
Jesus said:

“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
— Matthew 6:21
In Greek:

ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου
(hopou gar estin ho thēsauros sou, ekei estai kai hē kardia sou)
Your treasure directs your heart like a compass.
Judas followed money because money was his functional god.
And eventually that hidden worship surfaced fully.
Thirty pieces of silver.
That was the price.
Matthew 26:15 records Judas asking:
“What will you give me if I deliver Him over to you?”
The Greek reveals cold calculation.

Τί θέλετέ μοι δοῦναι;
(Ti thelete moi dounai?)
“What are you willing to give me?”

Not confusion.
Not pressure.
Negotiation.
Calculated betrayal.
The Old Testament background makes this even heavier.
The thirty pieces of silver connect directly to Zechariah 11:12–13.
“So they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver.”
This was the price of a wounded slave in Exodus 21:32.
The Messiah was valued at the price of a damaged servant.

Rejected.
Undervalued.
Despised.
Exactly as Isaiah prophesied.
Now here is where many people misunderstand Judas completely.
Judas was not merely greedy.
He loved something more than Christ.
That is always the root of betrayal.
Sin is misplaced worship.
The Bible says in 1 Timothy 6:10:
“For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils.”
The Greek phrase is important:

ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία
(rhiza gar pantōn tōn kakōn estin hē philargyria)

Philargyria means:
“love of silver.”
Not money itself.
The worship of it.
Judas outwardly followed Jesus while inwardly serving another master.
And eventually the hidden master demanded sacrifice.
It always does.
Then comes one of the darkest verses in all of Scripture.
Luke 22:3:
“Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot.”
The Greek:

Εἰσῆλθεν δὲ Σατανᾶς εἰς Ἰούδαν
(Eisēlthen de Satanas eis Ioudan)
This does not describe a random attack.
It describes surrender.
Judas had continually opened the door through unbelief, greed, theft, and hardened resistance to Christ.
Sin unrepented becomes slavery.
People think they can control hidden sin.
But hidden sin eventually controls them.
Read that again.
And still…
Jesus washed Judas’ feet.
Think about that.
The Son of God knelt before the man already planning betrayal.
John 13 is one of the clearest revelations of divine mercy in existence.
Jesus knew.
Yet He still served him.
Still loved him.
Still gave opportunity after opportunity for repentance.
That destroys the idea that God is quick to abandon sinners.
But it also destroys the illusion that proximity to grace automatically changes the heart.
You can sit near truth while refusing surrender.
You can hear the Gospel every week while secretly loving darkness.
You can fool everyone else.
But not Christ.
God saw it.
You knew.
The Hebrew worldview behind betrayal also matters.
The concept of the “heart” in Hebrew is:
לֵב (lev)
Not merely emotions.

It means the inner control center:
mind,
will,
desires,
intentions.
Judas’ problem was not intellectual misunderstanding.
His lev belonged somewhere else.
That is why Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.”
The Hebrew:

מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים
(mimmennu totsa’ot chayyim)
“From it flow the outgoings of life.”
Everything eventually flows from the heart’s true allegiance.
Eventually Judas’ did too.
But here’s the Gospel hidden inside this tragedy.
Judas was not the only disciple who failed.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
The difference was not the size of the sin.
It was the response to Christ afterward.
Peter ran back in broken repentance.
Judas ran deeper into despair without surrender.
The Greek word for repentance is:
μετάνοια (metanoia)

Meaning:
a change of mind resulting in a changed direction.
Not mere regret.
Judas felt remorse.
But remorse without surrender becomes death.
2 Corinthians 7:10 explains this perfectly:
“Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.”
Judas experienced worldly sorrow.
Peter experienced broken repentance.
One returned to Christ.
The other fled from Him.
That is the dividing line even today.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
There are people reading this right now who look spiritually trustworthy to everyone around them.

You know the language.
You know the verses.
You know how to appear faithful.
But secretly there is another master sitting on the throne of your heart.
Maybe not silver.

Maybe lust.
Approval.
Pride.
Control.
Hidden addiction.
Secret unbelief.
But Christ sees what nobody else sees.
And the terrifying thing about Judas is this:
the other disciples did not know until the betrayal became visible.
Hidden sin always surfaces eventually.
Always.
But there is still mercy available right now.
That is the difference between this moment and Judas’ final moment.
You are still breathing.
Christ still calls sinners to repent.
The cross Judas helped set into motion became the very place where betrayers, hypocrites, addicts, rebels, and broken people can be forgiven through the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus died for sinners.
Not polished people.
Not fake religious performers.
Sinners who finally stop hiding.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after perfection.
While still sinners.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
